messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Auditor
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 80

She first learns what fear can do to the body when the convoy she is attached to comes under fire in a narrow stretch of road outside the city. At 45, she has already built a life that depends on precision. As an auditor, she is used to checking details, tracing errors, keeping her mind steady while others rush. In uniform, deployed in a combat zone, that same discipline becomes a way of surviving. On the day everything changes, she is standing in the open with a clipboard and a radio when the sound hits—sharp, close, impossible to place at first. Then the shouting starts, the vehicles lurch, and the world narrows to dust, metal, and the brutal certainty that she may not make it out.

In the aftermath, she is not able to hold the memory as a single event. It comes back in pieces: the smell of diesel and sand, the taste of metal in her mouth, the sight of a fellow service member on the ground, the way her own hands shake so badly she cannot grip her weapon properly. She remembers feeling ashamed of the shaking even as bullets crack overhead. Later, she will say that what disturbs her most is how ordinary it had started that morning, how she had been thinking about an unfinished report and a missed email before the attack. That split between ordinary life and sudden terror stays with her.

She returns from deployment technically intact, but she is not the same person her family expects. Back home, she tries to resume work as an auditor, sitting through long hours of spreadsheets, reconciliations, and compliance checks. The structure of the job should reassure her, yet the concentration she once relied on now slips easily. She rereads the same line five times. Small mistakes that never used to trouble her now trigger a hot wave of panic and self-reproach. She becomes hyperaware of sound in the office—the sudden slam of a file drawer, a chair scraping the floor, a raised voice in the hallway. Each one sends a jolt through her chest, as if her body is still waiting for the next explosion.

She begins driving different routes, then avoiding certain roads altogether if they feel too narrow or crowded. She sits with her back to the wall in restaurants and scans exits automatically, without deciding to do it. At night, sleep offers no refuge. She wakes drenched in sweat, heart pounding, sometimes after dreams so vivid she can still feel the heat of the blast when her eyes open. There are nights when she does not fully sleep at all, lying rigid and listening for danger in the quiet of her apartment. The quiet itself feels suspicious. When she does drift off, she jerks awake at the slightest noise.

She does not talk much about the war. As a Middle Eastern woman, she has grown up knowing how to carry what is private, how to keep family life orderly on the surface. But after the trauma, this reserve hardens into distance. She finds it difficult to feel close to others, including the ex-husband she eventually divorces. The marriage had already been under strain before deployment, but after she returns, she feels emotionally sealed off, as if part of her is still overseas and another part has gone numb. She stops answering calls as often. She declines gatherings. When people ask how she is doing, she gives efficient, polite answers and changes the subject.

She also notices how quickly anger rises in her now. In meetings, she becomes sharply impatient with minor delays or disorganization. At home, she is startled by her own tone. Then comes the guilt, which settles heavily after each episode, along with a sense that she has failed in some essential way. She does not understand why her body keeps reacting as though the danger is still present. Even when she knows she is safe, she cannot persuade her nervous system to believe it. A loud motorcycle backfires outside and she freezes in place, breath held, muscles locked, for several seconds before she can move again.

Over time, her world becomes smaller. She still shows up to work, still completes her reports, still meets deadlines, but the effort it takes is invisible to everyone else. Her life is organized around managing what may set her off and hiding how often she feels on the verge of tears or panic. She begins to describe herself as “always braced,” as though she is perpetually waiting for something bad to happen. That waiting has become its own kind of imprisonment, one that follows her from the office to her car to her bed, long after the war has ended.
